questions.q: Describe the causes and course of the Non-Cooperation Movement.

answer.text: After the First World War, high taxes and prices caused hardship. The Rowlatt Act of 1919 allowed detention without trial, and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, in which General Dyer fired on an unarmed crowd at Amritsar, caused deep anger. The Khilafat issue also united Hindus and Muslims against the British.

Launched by Gandhi in 1920, the Non-Cooperation Movement called on Indians to boycott British schools, courts, titles and foreign cloth, and to promote swadeshi. Millions took part across the country. However, when a mob killed policemen at Chauri Chaura in 1922, Gandhi, committed to non-violence, called off the movement.

answer: Though halted, it showed the power of mass, non-violent struggle.

questions.q: How did a sense of collective belonging develop during the national movement?
answer: Nationalism grew not only through struggles but also through a shared sense of belonging created by symbols, culture and history.

answer.text: The nation was imagined as Bharat Mata, a figure first painted by Abanindranath Tagore, giving people a devotional image of their motherland.
Songs such as Vande Mataram, written by Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, stirred patriotic feeling, and the Swaraj flag with the spinning wheel became a symbol of unity and defiance.
The collection of folk tales and a reinterpretation of India's past instilled pride in its heritage.

answer: Together these symbols helped people across regions, classes and communities to feel part of one nation.

questions.q: How did the different social groups participate in the Civil Disobedience Movement, and what were their hopes?

answer.text: of 1930 drew in many groups, each joining for its own reasons and hopes.

list: Rich peasants joined against high revenue demands and were bitter when it was not reduced
Poor peasants wanted their unpaid rents to landlords remitted
Business classes wanted protection from imports and freedom to trade, and funded the movement
Women came out in large numbers to march, picket shops and make salt
But some groups, like the Dalits and many workers, stayed distant as their specific demands were not fully addressed

questions.q: Why did Mahatma Gandhi choose salt as the symbol for the Civil Disobedience Movement?

answer.text: chose salt as the focus of the movement because it was a brilliant unifying symbol.

list: Salt is used by every household — rich and poor, of every religion and region
The British monopoly and tax on salt was a hardship felt by all Indians

answer.text: It united the nation against an unjust law.

list: In 1930 Gandhi marched to Dandi and broke the law by making salt from seawater
The simple, non-violent act let ordinary people everywhere defy the government, turning the movement into a mass struggle
